Madarosis is a classic and relatively specific sign of facial nerve (especially great auricular and facial nerve) involvement in leprosy—not seen in vitiligo, pityriasis alba, or post-inflammatory hypopigmentation. The positive anti-PGL-1 antibody is highly specific for *Mycobacterium leprae* infection (though sensitivity is lower in paucibacillary disease); its presence strengthens the diagnosis, especially when combined with granulomatous histopathology on skin biopsy—a hallmark finding. Electrophysiologic evidence of early peripheral neuropathy (reduced ulnar SNAPs, mild grip weakness) confirms neural invasion, a sine qua non of leprosy (distinguishing it from purely dermatologic mimics). Critically, the absence of systemic symptoms, negative exclusionary workup for HIV/TB/vitiligo, and epidemiologic plausibility (rural U.S. setting—known endemic foci exist in Texas, Louisiana, Florida) further support leprosy over alternatives. While slit-skin smear is pending (and expected to be negative in paucibacillary disease), the constellation of clinical, serologic, histologic, and neurophysiologic findings meets WHO diagnostic criteria for leprosy: *at least one of*: (1) definite skin lesion with definite sensory loss, (2) positive skin smear, or (3) histologic evidence of granulomatous inflammation with neural involvement — all satisfied here.
